A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AL-RNN study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original AL-RNN experiments on classification, memory, contextual integration, SCAN, and joint modeling of rodent behavior and neural recordings.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds multi-task learning, variable-delay recall, baseline comparisons, and additional diagnostic experiments.

M1.justification: The core AL-RNN recurrence, regularization, and decoding framework remain. v2 extends the activation choices beyond ReLU to GeLU, tanh, and hardtanh, and implements final-layer-only nonlinear variants of S4 and Linear Transformers (Section 3; Figure 27). These are limited architectural extensions.

E1.justification: v2 adds an 11-task cognitive suite involving pro/anti responses, delayed matching, selective attention, and go/no-go decisions under joint training (Section 4.5; Appendix A.3). It also adds variable-delay copying, which changes recall timing requirements (A.4.3). The original datasets remain, including the relocated rodent experiment.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct LSTM and GRU comparisons on Addition, Copy, sMNIST, and Speech Commands in Table 2, substantially expanding v1's comparisons among AL-RNN configurations. Tables 2–3 add activation variants. Figure 27 separately compares fully linear, standard, and sparsely nonlinear configurations within S4 and Linear Transformers.

E3.justification: New protocols include multi-task training with 20, 50, or 500 samples per task, Jensen-Shannon comparisons of task representations, and additional latent-size/regularization controls (Figures 5 and 17). Appendix A.1.3 also changes the stated audio sequence-length comparison from 16k to 784 steps; this documentation change does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's bitcode and manifold analyses, v2 adds activation comparisons, training-loss and gradient diagnostics, train–test checks for overfitting, and best-run analyses (Tables 2–3; Figures 14, 17–18). It also adds digit-specific eigenspectra, stroke-aligned switching, multi-task representation consistency, and architecture-transfer analyses (Figures 9, 11, 24, 27).

E5.justification: v1 already reports ten-seed standard deviations and some SEM-based uncertainty. v2 adds an IMDb Welch's test (t = -1.34, p = 0.20), SCAN mean absolute deviation in Figure 18c, and explicit five-run aggregation for multi-task experiments. There is no reported increase in the retained experiments' ten-seed counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial multi-task, variable-delay, activation, and architecture results. Table 2 adds Copy accuracies of 54 ± 12% for LSTM and 69 ± 7% for GRU, alongside 92 ± 3% for ReLU AL-RNN. Figure 18 additionally reports that the best individual Addition model is fully nonlinear, qualifying the earlier emphasis on its poorer aggregate performance.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4.1 adds Proposition 1 and a formal impossibility proof for linear AL-RNNs solving masked addition. It derives the affine input–output mapping and shows that fixed coefficients cannot implement mask-dependent selection. v1 asserted this limitation without the corresponding proof.

C1.justification: v2 adds shared multi-task representations, computational reuse, and sample efficiency as central contributions in the abstract, introduction, and discussion. It qualifies v1's broad emphasis on minimal nonlinearity being often optimal by identifying low-data and switching-dependent settings where sparse nonlinearity is advantageous.

C2.justification: v2 shifts the explanation of fully nonlinear failures from overfitting/over-approximation toward optimization instability and learned linearization. It adds computational-reuse interpretations and specific limits on extending dynamical interpretability to modern architectures. However, Section 4.4's claim of chance-level linear performance on the rodent task conflicts with A.4.5, which retains successful task-only linear models and approximately 87% joint-model accuracy.

D1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated Reproducibility section providing a study-specific experiment/dataset repository; v1 only linked upstream AL-RNN implementation code. It also documents the new cognitive-task construction and the activation placement and causal implementation of the S4/Linear Transformer variants. The repository's availability is reported by the PDF.

R1.justification: v2 expands related work to Legendre Memory Units and hybrid sequence architectures, and adds references supporting multi-task motifs, linear attention, and piecewise-linear approximation. The central positioning remains repurposing the existing AL-RNN for mechanistic analysis. Several other reference changes are publication-metadata updates rather than new works.

P1.justification: The abstract, method exposition, and discussion undergo extensive rewriting, with revised terminology and a new title. Detailed classification, contextual-integration, and rodent analyses are redistributed into a reorganized appendix, while multi-task learning becomes a main section. The later discussion also contains a nearly duplicated paragraph.

P2.justification: v1's appendix model schematic becomes an expanded main Figure 1; IMDb and sMNIST displays are merged into v2 Figure 2. Contextual and rodent figures move to the appendix. v2 adds three tables and numerous diagnostic and multi-task figures, expands existing panels, and adopts a different publication layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's largely descriptive case: activation and hyperparameter controls, optimization diagnostics, and train–test analyses test alternative explanations for sparse nonlinearity's benefits. Multi-task experiments establish important data-dependent boundaries, while the addition proof and study-specific code-access information improve support and reproducibility. The contradictory rodent-task summary and limited baseline-setting details temper these gains, but the stronger evidence and more qualified explanations provide a substantial net improvement.
